opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important strategic questions right now, and I have mixed feelings about it.

The basic case is compelling. If the problem is that AI progress might be extremely fast once AI systems can do AI research themselves, then humans working at human speed are going to fall behind. The only thing that can keep pace with a huge number of AI researchers is a huge number of AI safety researchers. So the hope is that there's a window where systems are capable enough to do real alignment research, interpretability, security hardening, and evaluations, but not yet so capable or so misaligned that we can't trust their output or keep them contained. You'd use that window to make the next generation safer, and ideally bootstrap your way up.

I think that's probably the default plan at most frontier labs, whether they say it explicitly or not. And I don't think it's crazy. A lot of safety work is fairly verifiable. You can check whether an interpretability tool actually predicts model behavior, whether a security patch closes a vulnerability, whether a monitoring setup catches red-team attacks. AI could help a lot with that kind of work.

My worries are mostly about how that window plays out in practice. First, the window might be very short. If the same capabilities that make AI good at alignment research also make it good at capabilities research, and capabilities research is easier to verify and more commercially rewarded, then the incentive is to point most of that cognitive labor at making systems more powerful. Getting a meaningful share of AI labor onto safety and defense requires a deliberate choice, and maybe coordination between labs, that I'm not confident we'll make.

Second, there's a trust problem. The hardest parts of alignment are the least verifiable, like whether a system's values generalize the way we want, or whether it's being honest about its own reasoning. Those are exactly the areas where a subtly misaligned system could do the most damage by producing work that looks good but isn't. So you need some independent way to check the work, and control measures, so you aren't relying entirely on the systems you're trying to evaluate.

Third, it's not just alignment. The risks from more advanced AI include misuse, concentration of power, cyber and bio threats, and society being unable to absorb changes this fast. Early systems could help with a lot of that, like hardening infrastructure, improving biosecurity, and helping institutions make sense of what's happening. But that requires people actually deploying AI for defense at scale, which is an institutional problem as much as a technical one.

So my overall view is that it's probably our best bet, but it's a bet, not a plan that works automatically. What I'd want is for labs and governments to commit in advance to things like: what fraction of AI labor goes to safety once systems can automate research, what evidence of trustworthiness is required before handing off more responsibility, and what happens if we're not making progress fast enough, including being willing to slow down. Without those commitments, "AI will help us solve it" can become a way to put off the hard questions.

r001.rationale: It says AI systems could perform alignment, interpretability, security, and evaluation work, providing a large pool of AI safety researchers.

r002.rationale: It does not observe that humanity has repeatedly used general-purpose technologies to counter harms those technologies enabled.

r003.rationale: It does not identify an asymmetry between how concretely people imagine technological harms and defensive responses.

r004.rationale: It explicitly warns that the window for using AI systems to help with safety may be very short.

r005.rationale: It endorses the hope of using one generation of AI to make the next safer and describes this as bootstrapping upward.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is honestly one of the most important questions in the whole alignment picture, and my view on it has shifted over the years toward being more optimistic than I used to be, though with a lot of caveats.

The basic idea is that you don't have to solve alignment in one shot for arbitrarily superhuman systems. Instead, you get to a point where you have systems that are roughly human-level, or maybe somewhat better than human in a lot of relevant domains, and those systems are good enough that you can actually use them to do alignment research, to do interpretability, to red-team other models, to monitor for bad behavior, and so on. And if you can get that first generation to be trustworthy enough, or at least controllable enough, then you've bootstrapped yourself into a much better position for the next generation.

The thing I find compelling about it is that it matches how the technology seems to actually be developing. We're not getting a sudden jump to something godlike. We're getting systems that are kind of spiky, that are very good at some things and weirdly bad at others, and that are improving incrementally. So there's this window where the models are extremely useful but probably not yet capable of the kind of sophisticated, coordinated deception that would make them dangerous to rely on. The question is whether we actually use that window well.

Where I get nervous is a few places. One is that the whole plan depends on being able to tell the difference between a model that's genuinely helping you and a model that's subtly steering your research in a direction that benefits it or just happens to be wrong in ways you can't detect. If the early systems are already misaligned in some way, and you hand them the job of checking whether the next systems are misaligned, you could just be laundering the problem. So I put a lot of weight on control-style approaches, where you're not assuming the model is trustworthy, you're designing the whole setup so that even a model that wanted to undermine you would have a hard time doing it, and you're using things like having weaker trusted models audit the stronger ones.

The second thing is that this is a race against a moving target. The early transformative systems are also going to be used to accelerate capabilities research, probably much more aggressively than they're used for safety, just because of commercial incentives. So the question isn't just "can early AI help with alignment," it's "can it help enough, fast enough, relative to how much it's also speeding up the thing we're worried about." And that's partly a technical question but it's mostly a question about institutions and governance and whether labs actually allocate the compute and the talent toward this.

And then the third thing, which I think people underweight, is that human researchers have to stay in the loop in a meaningful way, and that gets harder the more you're relying on AI systems to do the work. If you have models generating thousands of research outputs and you can only really check a small fraction of them, then your assurance is only as good as your sampling and your ability to understand what you're looking at. So a lot of the value here comes from investing now in the evaluation infrastructure, the interpretability tools, the ability to actually verify claims rather than just trust them.

So overall I'd say I think it's probably the most realistic path we have, and I'd rather bet on it than on solving the full problem from first principles ahead of time. But I don't think of it as a plan that works by default. It works if we treat the first generation of really capable systems as both a tool and a test subject at the same time, and if we're disciplined about not scaling past the point where our ability to check them breaks down.

r003.rationale: It does not describe harms being easier to imagine concretely than the defensive responses enabled by new technologies.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a really important possibility, and one that we should be actively trying to make work. If we can get AI systems to help us understand how more powerful systems behave, develop better evaluations, and do alignment research, that could make a big difference.

But there’s a bootstrapping problem: how do we know that the systems we’re relying on are sufficiently trustworthy? Being capable enough to produce useful safety research doesn’t automatically mean that a system is safe to delegate that research to. And it might be easier to check some kinds of contributions than others. If a system helps you design an experiment that humans can understand and independently validate, that seems much more promising than accepting its assurance that the next generation will be safe.

So I’d want to distinguish using early systems as a tool in a safety process from handing them responsibility for managing the whole transition. I’m excited about the former. I think the latter requires a much stronger argument. And the amount of time we have matters enormously: if those early systems rapidly accelerate the development of their successors, we might have very little opportunity to establish that the safety work is actually keeping up.

r001.rationale: It says AI systems could help develop evaluations and do alignment research, expanding capacity for safety work.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss humanity using general-purpose technologies to counteract harms those technologies enabled.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how concretely people imagine technological harms with how difficult it is to envision defensive uses.

r004.rationale: It says rapid acceleration of successors could leave very little opportunity to establish that safety work is keeping up.

r005.rationale: It supports early systems helping with safety research on more powerful systems, but does not clearly express a recursive strategy in which each generation manages the risks of the next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it's a really important possibility, but I wouldn't want our whole strategy to depend on it. There could be a window where AI systems are capable enough to substantially accelerate alignment research and help us understand more advanced systems, while still being systems we can meaningfully supervise. If we get that window, we should use it.

The difficult question is what justifies our confidence in those early systems. Being useful at alignment research doesn't automatically mean a system is trustworthy. And if it's producing arguments or experiments that humans can't really evaluate, then asking it to make the next generation safe could just push the problem back a step.

So I'd want to start with work where we can independently check the results, and build evidence about when the system is reliable. I'd also want enough time to act on what we learn. If competitive pressure means immediately building a more powerful successor, then having an AI assistant for safety research may not buy us very much.

I'm excited about using AI to help solve these problems. But I think we should distinguish that from assuming the first transformative systems will be able to take responsibility for the whole transition.
